title: http command creates a fresh HttpClient and handler per step — no connection reuse in loops, and timeouts over 100s silently broken
existing_state: Every execution of an http: step constructs a new HttpClientHandler and HttpClient inside using blocks (Services/Scripting/Commands/HttpCommand.cs:92-93, handler built at 320-333) and disposes them when the step ends. In a foreach/while polling loop or a multi-host run, each request pays a full TCP + TLS handshake and leaves a socket in TIME_WAIT; nothing is pooled or reused — the textbook HttpClient anti-pattern, where sustained tight polling can exhaust ephemeral ports. A side effect of the per-step client: the default HttpClient.Timeout of 100s is never overridden, so a step declaring timeout: 300 (HttpCommand.cs:90, 94-95 only sets the CTS) is silently capped at ~100s by the client's own timeout, then misreported as having timed out after the configured seconds (192-196).
recommendation: Cache clients keyed by handler-affecting options — (VerifyTls, FollowRedirects) is the full key today — in a small static ConcurrentDictionary<(bool,bool), HttpClient> (or one SocketsHttpHandler with PooledConnectionLifetime ~2 min per key). Set client.Timeout = Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan and keep the existing per-step linked-CTS timeout (94-95), which also fixes the 100s cap on long timeout: values. The injectable _handlerFactory test seam (45-48) can stay; only the default path needs caching.
user_benefit: Scripts that poll REST APIs in loops or fan HTTP calls across a fleet run noticeably faster (one TLS handshake instead of one per request) and stop risking ephemeral-port exhaustion on long runs; per-step timeouts over 100 seconds actually work.

evidence.note: fresh handler+client pair per step; CTS timeout layered on top of the default 100s client timeout
CreateDefaultHandler — only FollowRedirects and VerifyTls vary, so a 2-key client cache covers all cases
timeout catch reports the step's configured seconds even when the client's built-in 100s timeout fired first
